categories.description: Specimens, organs, pinned structures and functions.

categories.description: Recognize tissues, cells, layers and identification points.

stations.title: Find the sternal angle

parts.prompt: Name the junction forming the sternal angle.
parts.answer: Manubriosternal joint: junction of manubrium and body.

parts.prompt: Give its rib and vertebral landmarks.
parts.answer: Second costal cartilage; T4–T5 intervertebral disc.

stations.remember: Palpate the angle, find rib 2, then count spaces. The tracheal bifurcation is near this plane.

stations.title: Orient the sternum

parts.prompt: Name its three main parts from superior to inferior.
Which superior notches articulate with the clavicles?
parts.answer: The right and left clavicular notches of the manubrium.

stations.remember: The jugular notch is midline; the paired clavicular notches are lateral.

stations.title: Classify ribs

parts.prompt: Give the true, vertebrochondral and floating rib ranges.
Which ribs are typical?

stations.remember: Atypical ribs are 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12. False ribs broadly include 8–12; floating ribs are a subgroup.

stations.title: Orient a typical rib

parts.prompt: Name the head, neck, tubercle and angle and locate the costal groove.
parts.answer: Head is posterior; neck connects head to tubercle; angle is the bend; costal groove is on the internal inferior border.

parts.prompt: What does the costal groove protect, from superior to inferior?

stations.remember: Orient the concavity medially and costal groove inferiorly before assigning a side.

stations.title: First rib grooves

parts.prompt: Which vessel passes anterior to the scalene tubercle?
Which vessel passes posterior to it?

stations.remember: The anterior scalene attaches to the scalene tubercle. Do not swap artery and vein.

stations.title: Recognize atypical ribs

parts.prompt: Which two ribs lack a neck and tubercle?
What identifies rib 2 on its superior surface?
parts.answer: The rough tuberosity for serratus anterior.

stations.remember: Floating ribs have no costotransverse articulation; rib 1 is short, broad and flattened.

stations.title: Thoracic vertebra identification

parts.prompt: Give two features supporting a thoracic vertebra identification.
parts.answer: Costal facets for ribs and a long inferiorly directed spinous process; typically a heart-shaped body.

parts.prompt: What articulates with the transverse costal facet?
parts.answer: The tubercle of the corresponding rib (for ribs with a costotransverse joint).

stations.remember: The head articulates with bodies; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process.

stations.title: Articulate a typical rib

parts.prompt: Which bodies articulate with the head of rib 5?
parts.answer: T4 and T5, with the intervening disc.

parts.prompt: Which transverse process articulates with its tubercle?

stations.remember: A typical rib head meets its own vertebra and the vertebra above; tubercle meets the same-number transverse process.

stations.title: Surface reference lines

parts.prompt: How do you trace the midclavicular line?
parts.answer: Vertically through the midpoint of the clavicle.

parts.prompt: How do midaxillary and scapular lines differ?
parts.answer: Midaxillary passes through the midpoint of the axilla; scapular passes through the inferior angle of the scapula with the arms by the side.

stations.remember: Use the requested reference line before quoting a lung, pleural or cardiac surface level.

stations.title: Anterior interventricular territory

parts.prompt: Which artery runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus?
Which portion of the septum does it usually supply?
parts.answer: Anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

stations.remember: LAD septal branches supply anterior two-thirds; PDA septal branches supply posterior one-third.
stations.correction: Week 2 guide p32 reverses the septal fractions. Corrected using its own p6–7 and the primary anatomical references recorded in the source review.

stations.title: Follow the left coronary system

parts.prompt: Name the two principal branches of the left coronary artery.
Which sulcus does circumflex follow?

stations.remember: LAD descends between ventricles; circumflex wraps between left atrium and ventricle.
stations.correction: The guide p29 says circumflex is not a branch; this conflicts with p7 and standard anatomy. Use LAD and circumflex as the main branches.

stations.title: Trace the right coronary artery

parts.prompt: Give the origin of the RCA.
parts.answer: Right aortic sinus of the ascending aorta.

parts.prompt: Name two major branches in a right-dominant heart.
parts.answer: Right marginal artery and posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery.

stations.remember: RCA follows the right AV groove. PDA origin determines dominance, not artery size.

stations.title: Determine coronary dominance

parts.prompt: What defines coronary dominance?
parts.answer: The coronary artery giving rise to the PDA.

parts.prompt: In left dominance, where does the PDA arise?
parts.answer: Circumflex branch of the left coronary artery.

stations.remember: Never assume every posterior septal supply is from the RCA: establish the dominance pattern.

stations.title: Pair coronary arteries and veins

parts.prompt: Which vein accompanies the LAD?
Which vein accompanies the PDA?

stations.remember: Great cardiac vein follows anterior interventricular sulcus then left AV groove; middle follows posterior interventricular sulcus.

stations.title: Coronary sinus drainage

parts.prompt: Where does the coronary sinus open?
Name two tributaries.
parts.answer: Great cardiac vein and middle cardiac vein; small cardiac vein is also acceptable.

stations.remember: The coronary sinus lies posteriorly in the AV groove. Anterior cardiac veins bypass it.

stations.title: Direct venous drainage

parts.prompt: Where do anterior cardiac veins drain?
Where do the smallest (Thebesian) cardiac veins drain?

stations.remember: Not all cardiac veins drain through the coronary sinus.

stations.title: Mediastinal compartments

parts.prompt: Give the plane dividing superior from inferior mediastinum.
parts.answer: Sternal angle to the T4–T5 disc.

parts.prompt: Name the three inferior compartments from anterior to posterior.

stations.remember: The pericardium and heart occupy the middle compartment; the space behind contains oesophagus and descending aorta.

stations.title: Aortic arch branches

parts.prompt: List the three branches from anatomical right to left.
parts.answer: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.

parts.prompt: What branches arise from the brachiocephalic trunk?
parts.answer: Right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

stations.remember: The left common carotid arises directly from the arch in the standard pattern.

stations.title: Nerves at the lung root

parts.prompt: Which nerve passes anterior to the lung root?
Which passes posterior and contributes to the oesophageal plexus?

stations.remember: Phrenic runs between mediastinal pleura and pericardium and supplies diaphragm motor fibres.

stations.title: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve

parts.prompt: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loop?
parts.answer: Under the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum.

parts.prompt: What voice change can compression cause?
parts.answer: Hoarseness due to impaired laryngeal muscle function.

stations.remember: Ligamentum arteriosum is the adult remnant of the ductus arteriosus.

stations.title: Azygos system

parts.prompt: Where does the azygos vein drain?
Name the lower and upper left-sided veins crossing to it.

stations.remember: Orient right versus left before naming an azygos-system vessel.

stations.title: Thoracic sympathetic chain

parts.prompt: Where is the thoracic sympathetic trunk located?
Where do thoracic splanchnic nerves carry predominantly sympathetic fibres?
parts.answer: Toward abdominal viscera through prevertebral pathways.

stations.remember: Damage to the upper sympathetic pathway can produce ipsilateral Horner syndrome; a generic thoracic chain label alone does not establish the lesion level.

stations.title: Intercostal neurovascular plane

parts.prompt: State the main bundle order from superior to inferior.
Between which muscle layers does it travel?

stations.remember: The main bundle lies in the costal groove beneath a rib. Recognize the plane on a specimen.

stations.title: Posterior intercostal supply

parts.prompt: Where do posterior intercostal arteries 1–2 originate?
parts.answer: Supreme intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk.

parts.prompt: Where do posterior arteries 3–11 originate?

stations.remember: The subcostal artery runs below rib 12, outside the 11 intercostal spaces.

stations.title: Anterior intercostal supply

parts.prompt: What supplies anterior spaces 1–6?
What supplies anterior spaces 7–9?

stations.remember: There are no anterior intercostal arteries in spaces 10–11.

stations.title: Internal thoracic termination

parts.prompt: Name the two terminal branches.
Which continues into the rectus sheath?

stations.remember: Musculophrenic follows the costal margin and contributes to diaphragmatic and lower anterior intercostal supply.

stations.title: Atypical intercostal nerves

parts.prompt: Which nerve forms the intercostobrachial nerve?
Which intercostal nerves continue into the abdominal wall?

stations.remember: T1 largely joins the brachial plexus; T12 is subcostal, not an intercostal nerve.

stations.title: Intercostal venous return

parts.prompt: Where do upper anterior intercostal veins drain?
Where do lower posterior intercostal veins drain?
parts.answer: Into the azygos system on the right and hemiazygos/accessory hemiazygos pathways on the left.

stations.remember: Venous routes vary by space and side: do not say every intercostal vein drains directly into the SVC.

stations.title: Intercostal muscle layers

parts.prompt: Name the three main intercostal muscle layers superficial to deep.
Which nerve supplies them?

stations.remember: External intercostals assist inspiration. Internal interosseous fibres assist forced expiration; internal interchondral fibres can elevate ribs.
stations.correction: Week 5 p5 repeats subcostales attachments for innermost intercostals. These are not treated as interchangeable muscles.

stations.title: Orient the heart

parts.prompt: Which chamber forms most of the anterior surface?
Which chamber forms most of the base?

stations.remember: The apex is left ventricle; the right border is right atrium; the diaphragmatic surface is mainly left ventricle.

stations.title: Locate the cardiac apex

parts.prompt: Which chamber forms the apex?
Give its usual surface landmark.
parts.answer: Left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

stations.remember: State side, intercostal space and reference line together.

stations.title: Pericardial layers

parts.prompt: Which serous layer covers the heart directly?
Where is the pericardial cavity?
parts.answer: Between parietal and visceral serous pericardium.

stations.remember: Fibrous pericardium is the tough outer sac; parietal serous pericardium lines its inner surface.

stations.title: Transverse pericardial sinus

parts.prompt: Name the passage behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
Which great vessels lie anterior to it?

stations.remember: The transverse sinus is open at both ends and permits surgical passage behind the arterial outflow vessels.

stations.title: Oblique pericardial sinus

parts.prompt: Which chamber lies immediately anterior to this blind recess?
Which venous reflections bound it?
parts.answer: Reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava.

stations.remember: Unlike the transverse sinus, the oblique sinus is a blind-ended pouch behind the left atrium.

stations.title: Right atrial landmarks

parts.prompt: What ridge separates smooth from pectinate regions?
Which opening is associated with the Eustachian valve?

stations.remember: The Thebesian valve guards the coronary sinus opening. The Eustachian valve is not a valve of the SVC.
stations.correction: Week 2 p17 incorrectly associates the Eustachian valve with SVC; the correct vessel is IVC.

stations.title: Fossa ovalis and fetal flow

parts.prompt: Name the oval depression in the interatrial septum.
Which fetal communication does it mark?
parts.answer: Foramen ovale, which allowed right-to-left atrial flow.

stations.remember: The fossa is the postnatal remnant; the fetal foramen, not the adult fossa, carried the shunt.

stations.title: Right ventricular outflow

parts.prompt: Name the smooth RV outflow tract.
Which valve leads into the pulmonary trunk?

stations.remember: Trabeculae carneae mark the rough inflow region; the smooth conus leads toward the pulmonary valve.

stations.title: Moderator band

parts.prompt: Name the band crossing from septum toward anterior papillary muscle.
Which conducting tissue passes through it?
parts.answer: Part of the right bundle branch.

stations.remember: Do not confuse the moderator band with a chord: it is a muscular bridge containing conducting tissue.

stations.title: Papillary muscles and chordae

parts.prompt: What connects papillary muscles to AV valve cusps?
What is the function during ventricular systole?
parts.answer: Tension prevents AV valve prolapse into the atria.

stations.remember: Papillary muscles stabilize closed AV valves; they do not actively pull the valves open.

stations.title: Semilunar valve recognition

parts.prompt: Do semilunar valves have chordae tendineae?
Where do the coronary arteries originate relative to the aortic valve?
parts.answer: Right and left aortic sinuses behind the corresponding cusps.

stations.remember: Coronary ostia are in the aortic sinus walls, not holes through the valve leaflets.

stations.title: Left atrium and ventricle

parts.prompt: How many pulmonary veins usually enter the left atrium?
Name the smooth LV outflow toward the aorta.

stations.remember: Mitral valve has two leaflets and two papillary muscle groups; RV has tricuspid valve and typically three papillary groups.

stations.title: Interventricular septum

parts.prompt: Name the two main septal components.
parts.answer: Large muscular part and small membranous part.

parts.prompt: Which part is a common site of ventricular septal defect?

stations.remember: Do not memorize the guide’s one-third membranous fraction: the membranous region is small.

stations.title: Nasal drainage

parts.prompt: What drains into the inferior meatus?
Where does the sphenoid sinus drain?

stations.remember: Posterior ethmoidal cells drain into superior meatus; frontal, maxillary and anterior/middle ethmoidal pathways connect to middle meatus.

stations.title: Concha versus meatus

parts.prompt: Which is the projecting shelf: concha or meatus?
Where is its corresponding meatus?

stations.remember: Conchae increase surface area and turbulence; the septum is the smooth medial wall.

stations.title: Nasal septum

parts.prompt: Name its principal bony components.
parts.answer: Perpendicular plate of ethmoid and vomer.

parts.prompt: Where is Little’s area and why does it bleed readily?
parts.answer: Anterior septum; multiple arterial branches anastomose there.

stations.remember: Anterior septum also contains septal cartilage. Distinguish lateral conchae from medial septum.

stations.title: Nasopharyngeal landmarks

parts.prompt: What is the raised prominence at the auditory tube opening?
What lymphoid tissue lies in the roof/posterior wall?

stations.remember: The auditory tube connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear.

stations.title: Laryngeal cartilages

parts.prompt: Which laryngeal cartilage forms a complete ring?
Which cartilage bears the vocal and muscular processes?

stations.remember: True vocal ligaments attach posteriorly to vocal processes; intrinsic muscles act on muscular processes.

stations.title: True and false folds

parts.prompt: Name the space between vestibular and vocal folds.
What is the gap between the true vocal folds called?

stations.remember: Vestibular folds are superior to vocal folds; the vestibule extends from inlet to vestibular folds.

stations.title: Laryngeal muscle action

parts.prompt: Which muscle is the only abductor of the vocal folds?
Which nerve supplies cricothyroid?
parts.answer: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

stations.remember: All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles receive recurrent laryngeal motor supply. Cricothyroid tenses the folds.

stations.title: Tracheal orientation

parts.prompt: Give the usual beginning and bifurcation levels.
Which muscle bridges the posterior cartilage gap?

stations.remember: C-shaped hyaline rings are open posteriorly toward the oesophagus; the carina is at bifurcation.

stations.title: Right versus left main bronchus

parts.prompt: Which main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical?
How many lobar bronchi arise on each side?
parts.answer: Three on the right and two on the left.

stations.remember: Aspirated foreign bodies more often enter the right main bronchus; specify main versus lobar versus segmental.

stations.title: Side a lung

parts.prompt: Which lung has horizontal and oblique fissures?
Name two left-sided identifying features.

stations.remember: Three lobes on the right; two lobes on the left. A lingula is part of the left superior lobe.

stations.title: Pulmonary artery at the hilum

parts.prompt: Where is the right pulmonary artery relative to the main bronchus?
Where is the left pulmonary artery relative to the main bronchus?

stations.remember: RALS: Right Anterior, Left Superior. Inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest major hilar structure.

stations.title: Pulmonary vein drainage

parts.prompt: Which lobes drain into the right superior pulmonary vein?
Which lobe drains into the right inferior pulmonary vein?

stations.remember: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood into the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

stations.title: Pleural layers and recesses

parts.prompt: Which pleural layer enters the lung fissures?
Where does fluid commonly collect in an upright pleural cavity?

stations.remember: Costal, mediastinal, diaphragmatic and cervical pleura are parts of parietal pleura.

stations.title: Lung and pleural surface levels

parts.prompt: Give lung inferior border ribs at MCL, midaxillary and scapular lines.
Give parietal pleural inferior limits along the same lines.

stations.remember: These are rib levels in the usual surface projection, not a request to name the intercostal spaces.

stations.title: Root and pulmonary ligament

parts.prompt: What forms the pulmonary ligament?
parts.answer: The double pleural fold below the lung root.

parts.prompt: Name the principal airway and blood vessels in the root.
parts.answer: Bronchus, pulmonary artery and pulmonary veins.

stations.remember: The hilum is the surface doorway; the root is the bundle passing through it.

stations.title: Bronchopulmonary segments

parts.prompt: Name the right middle-lobe segments.
What airway supplies a bronchopulmonary segment?

stations.remember: Left basal segment names and fusion patterns vary. Use names and the actual specimen rather than the guide’s inconsistent left lower-lobe numbering.
stations.correction: Week 5 p28 gives a nonstandard left lower-lobe segment number list. It is not used as an answer key.

stations.title: Cardiac muscle identification

parts.prompt: Give two identifying features of cardiac muscle in longitudinal section.
parts.answer: Branching striated fibres with central nuclei; intercalated discs are another distinguishing feature.

parts.prompt: Which junction enables electrical coupling?

stations.remember: Desmosomes and adherens junctions provide mechanical attachment; gap junctions pass current.

stations.title: Epicardial surface

parts.prompt: Name the epithelium covering epicardium.
Name two structures often found in subepicardial fat.

stations.remember: Epicardium faces serous fluid; endocardium faces blood. Do not label both epithelia as endothelium.

stations.title: Endocardial surface

parts.prompt: Name the epithelium facing the ventricular lumen.
Which specialized cells lie in the deeper subendocardium?

stations.remember: Endothelium → subendothelial connective tissue → subendocardial connective tissue containing Purkinje fibres.

stations.title: Purkinje versus working myocytes

parts.prompt: Give two identifying features of Purkinje cells.
parts.answer: Large pale cells with abundant glycogen and relatively few peripheral myofibrils.

parts.prompt: State their function.
parts.answer: Rapid conduction of ventricular excitation to working myocardium.

stations.remember: Purkinje fibres are modified cardiac muscle, not peripheral nerves. Central nuclei can occur in both cell types.

stations.title: Cardiac wall layers

parts.prompt: List the wall layers from chamber lumen outward.
Why is the LV myocardium thicker than RV myocardium?
parts.answer: It generates the higher pressure needed for systemic circulation.

stations.remember: Both ventricles normally pump the same stroke volume; wall thickness reflects pressure load, not simply more blood volume.

stations.title: Elastic artery

parts.prompt: Identify a vessel with many concentric elastic lamellae in its media.
Give an example and functional name.

stations.remember: Elastic lamellae are numerous throughout media. A single prominent IEL suggests a muscular artery instead.

stations.title: Medium muscular artery

parts.prompt: What dominates its tunica media?
Name its two elastic boundaries.
parts.answer: Internal elastic lamina and external elastic lamina.

stations.remember: Muscular arteries distribute blood; IEL borders intima/media and EEL borders media/adventitia.

stations.title: Small muscular artery

parts.prompt: Give its characteristic elastic layer.
How does its companion vein differ?
parts.answer: Thinner media with fewer smooth-muscle layers and no comparable prominent IEL; more irregular lumen.

stations.remember: A small muscular artery has several smooth muscle layers, unlike an arteriole with one or two.

stations.title: Arteriole and venule

parts.prompt: How many smooth-muscle layers typify the lab arteriole?
Give a distinguishing feature from its accompanying venule.
parts.answer: Relatively thicker wall and rounder lumen; venule wall is thinner and lumen more collapsed.

stations.remember: The smallest arterioles lack a distinct IEL; larger arterioles may show one, so do not use its absence as a universal law.

stations.title: Capillary identification

parts.prompt: For a capillary in the connective tissue between these cardiac muscle fibres, what forms its wall?
What arrangement of red cells helps identify a narrow capillary?
parts.answer: Red cells passing in single file.

stations.remember: No tunica media, no adventitia and no smooth-muscle layer surround a typical capillary.

stations.title: Large vein

parts.prompt: Which tunic is thickest?
Which muscle orientation is prominent there, especially in IVC?

stations.remember: Distinguish circular media muscle from longitudinal adventitial bundles.

stations.title: Vasa vasorum

parts.prompt: Where are vasa vasorum mainly found?
parts.answer: Adventitia and outer wall of large vessels.

parts.prompt: What is their function?
parts.answer: Supply oxygen and nutrients to the outer vessel wall.

stations.remember: A small vessel is vasa vasorum only when it supplies the wall of a larger vessel.

stations.title: Continuous and fenestrated capillaries

parts.prompt: What distinguishes a fenestrated capillary from a continuous one?
Do both generally retain a continuous basal lamina?

stations.remember: Do not confuse endothelial fenestrae with a missing basal lamina.

stations.title: Respiratory nasal mucosa

parts.prompt: Give the full epithelial name.
parts.answer: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

parts.prompt: What do the goblet cells do?
parts.answer: Secrete mucus that traps inhaled particles.

stations.remember: Cilia move mucus; seromucous glands and vascular connective tissue lie beneath the epithelium.

stations.title: Olfactory mucosa

parts.prompt: Name the sensory cell type.
Name the glands in the lamina propria and their secretion.
parts.answer: Bowman glands; watery serous secretion that dissolves odorants.

stations.remember: Supporting and basal cells accompany olfactory neurons. Olfactory epithelium lacks goblet cells.

stations.title: Tracheal wall

parts.prompt: List its four main layers.
parts.answer: Mucosa, submucosa, hyaline cartilage layer, adventitia.

parts.prompt: What are the components of the mucosa?

stations.remember: Submucosal seromucous glands and hyaline cartilage support a tracheal identification.

stations.title: Intrapulmonary bronchus

parts.prompt: How does its cartilage differ from tracheal cartilage?
parts.answer: Irregular plates instead of C-shaped rings.

parts.prompt: What contractile layer lies beneath its mucosa?

stations.remember: Bronchus retains cartilage and glands; bronchiole lacks both.

stations.title: Conducting bronchiole

parts.prompt: Name two structures absent from a bronchiole wall.
What epithelial cell becomes prominent distally?
parts.answer: Club cell, alongside simple cuboidal ciliated cells.

stations.remember: Do not identify an airway only by lumen size: cartilage, glands and alveolar openings are more reliable.

stations.title: Respiratory bronchiole

parts.prompt: What distinguishes it from a terminal bronchiole?
What epithelium lines its non-alveolated portions?
parts.answer: Simple cuboidal epithelium with club cells, with fewer ciliated cells proximally.

stations.remember: Respiratory bronchioles begin the gas-exchanging zone; terminal bronchioles remain conducting.

stations.title: Type I and II pneumocytes

parts.prompt: Which cell is thin and specialized for gas diffusion?
Which cell secretes surfactant and regenerates alveolar epithelium?

stations.remember: Type II cells are cuboidal; type I cells spread thinly across most alveolar surface area.

stations.title: Alveolar duct and sac

parts.prompt: What identifies an alveolar duct?
parts.answer: An elongated passage whose walls consist largely of alveolar openings.

parts.prompt: What identifies an alveolar sac?
parts.answer: A common space into which a cluster of alveoli opens.

stations.remember: Alveoli are individual terminal air spaces; distinguish them from the shared duct or sac.

stations.title: Pleural histology

parts.prompt: Name the surface epithelial cell type.
Name the underlying tissue.
parts.answer: Thin connective tissue containing collagen and elastic fibres.

stations.remember: Mesothelium covers the lung surface; pneumocytes line alveoli. These are different surfaces.

stations.title: Choana and nasal floor

parts.prompt: What connects the nasal cavity to the nasopharynx?
Name its medial and inferior bony boundaries.
parts.answer: Vomer medially; horizontal plate of palatine bone inferiorly.

stations.remember: The lateral boundary is medial pterygoid plate. The hard palate forms the nasal floor.

stations.title: Middle meatus drainage

parts.prompt: Name two paranasal sinuses draining through the middle meatus region.
parts.answer: Maxillary and frontal sinuses; anterior and middle ethmoidal cells also drain into this region.

parts.prompt: Which ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus?

stations.remember: Inferior meatus receives nasolacrimal duct; sphenoid sinus drains into sphenoethmoidal recess above superior concha.

stations.title: Epiglottis

parts.prompt: Identify the leaf-shaped cartilage at the laryngeal inlet.
State its role during swallowing.
parts.answer: Helps protect the airway as the laryngeal inlet closes during swallowing.

stations.remember: It is upright during breathing and participates in airway protection during swallowing; closure also involves laryngeal elevation and vocal-fold mechanisms.

stations.title: Lung surfaces and borders

parts.prompt: Which surface bears the hilum?
Which border is thick and rounded, and which borders are sharp?
parts.answer: Posterior border is thick and rounded; anterior and inferior borders are sharp.

stations.remember: The concave base rests on the diaphragm; the apex projects into the root of the neck above the medial clavicle.

stations.title: Parts of parietal pleura

parts.prompt: Name the four parts of parietal pleura.
Where do parietal and visceral pleura become continuous?
parts.answer: Around the root of the lung.

stations.remember: The pulmonary ligament is the double pleural fold below the root; the potential cavity lies between parietal and visceral layers.

stations.title: Respiratory muscle action

parts.prompt: Which main intercostal layer elevates ribs during inspiration?
Which part of internal intercostals assists forced expiration?

stations.remember: Internal interchondral fibres can elevate ribs. Do not assign all internal intercostal fibres the same expiratory action.

stations.title: Myocardial connective tissue

parts.prompt: What connective tissue surrounds individual cardiac muscle cells?
How can you distinguish a fibroblast nucleus from an endothelial nucleus in this field?
parts.answer: Fibroblast nuclei lie between muscle fibres in connective tissue; endothelial nuclei form the wall of a capillary containing red blood cells.

stations.remember: Look for location, a capillary lumen and red cells. A dark elongated nucleus alone is insufficient for identification.

stations.title: Vascular smooth muscle function

parts.prompt: What is the main contractile cell in arterial media?
Besides contraction, what synthetic role does it have?
parts.answer: Synthesis of extracellular matrix, including collagen and other matrix components.

stations.remember: The media can contain collagen without visible fibroblasts; vascular smooth muscle has both contractile and synthetic roles.

stations.title: Vessel tunics

parts.prompt: List the three tunics from lumen outward.
parts.answer: Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica adventitia (externa).

parts.prompt: What epithelium lines the intima?
parts.answer: Simple squamous endothelium on a basal lamina.

stations.remember: Compare the relative thickness of media and adventitia rather than relying on lumen shape alone; section angle and collapse can distort it.

stations.title: Set up and zero before recording

parts.prompt: During zeroing a volunteer continues blowing through the flow head. What is the best correction?
parts.answer: Place the flow head undisturbed on the bench and re-zero

parts.prompt: How should the flow head be handled during zeroing?
parts.answer: Keep the flow head stationary and free of airflow during zeroing; follow the supplied device setup.

stations.remember: The flow head measures airflow; the software also displays volume. Before recording, leave the flow head undisturbed on the bench and select Spirometer Pod from the flow-channel function menu, then Zero. Movement or airflow during zeroing can bias the baseline. For quiet breathing, the handout asks the volunteer to face away from the screen so they do not consciously alter the pattern. Record normal tidal breathing for 20 seconds and annotate the trace. Equipment-specific steps here follow the supplied prelab, rather than being a universal device protocol.

stations.title: Read flow and volume; identify capacities

parts.prompt: Quiet volume readings alternate between0.15 and0.65 L. What is the tidal volume?
Which volumes or capacities cannot ordinary spirometry measure directly?
parts.answer: Residual volume, functional residual capacity and total lung capacity, because each includes residual gas.

stations.remember: Read the axes first. A flow trace reports rate (L/s); the volume trace reports an accumulated change in liters. Tidal volume is the peak-to-trough volume excursion during a quiet breath, not the height of a flow peak. After quiet breathing, a maximal inspiration above a normal inspiratory level demonstrates inspiratory reserve volume; maximal expiration below the resting expiratory level demonstrates expiratory reserve volume. IC=VT+IRV; VC=IRV+VT+ERV. Ordinary spirometry measures volume changes and cannot directly measure residual volume, FRC or TLC because each includes gas not exhaled into the spirometer.

stations.title: Perform and read forced expiration

parts.prompt: A forced expiration expels2.4 L in the first second and4.0 L in total. What is FEV1/FVC?
How do FEV1 and FVC differ?
parts.answer: FEV1 is the volume expired during the first second; FVC is the full volume expired in a forced vital-capacity maneuver.

stations.remember: The prelab asks for re-zeroing,30 seconds of normal breathing, maximal inspiration, then expiration as forcefully and fully as possible until no more air can be expelled. Record three separate forced breaths. The initial maximal inspiration and sustained expiration matter: a weak start or early stop can produce misleading numbers. FEV1 is the volume exhaled in the first second of the forced maneuver. FVC is the full forced vital capacity. On the supplied remaining-volume trace, both are downward differences from maximal inspiration, not absolute y-axis readings. FEV1/FVC=(first-second volume)/(total forced volume), expressed as a fraction or percent.

stations.title: Distinguish obstruction from suspected restriction

parts.prompt: A technically adequate test has FEV1/FVC below the provided lower limit of normal. Which pattern is supported?
Does a low FVC with a preserved ratio prove restriction?
parts.answer: No. Confirm restriction with a reduced TLC; poor effort or air trapping can also reduce FVC.

stations.remember: Obstruction makes rapid expiration difficult; FEV1 often falls disproportionately, lowering FEV1/FVC. A reduced FVC with a preserved ratio can suggest restriction but can also reflect poor effort or air trapping. Confirming restriction requires reduced TLC, measured with an appropriate lung-volume method. Use the measured ratio against an appropriate lower limit of normal and inspect recording quality. A single low value or a simplistic fixed cutoff is not a complete diagnosis. Dyspnea can also have cardiac, hematologic or deconditioning causes, so normal spirometry does not rule out all causes of breathlessness.

stations.title: Apply the supplied asthma case

parts.prompt: Which direct drug effect explains why albuterol was prescribed in the source case?
parts.answer: Relax airway smooth muscle through β2 receptor activation

parts.prompt: What spirometric pattern can active airflow obstruction produce?
parts.answer: FEV1 reduced disproportionately to FVC, lowering FEV1/FVC; actual measurements and quality checks are needed.

stations.remember: The case describes recurrent trigger-associated wheeze, increased attacks after infection and severe respiratory distress despite albuterol. Bronchial smooth muscle contraction, airway inflammation and mucus can obstruct expiratory airflow and promote air trapping. Albuterol is a β2-adrenergic agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle. A poor response in this case does not convert the process into restriction or identify a single cause of death from spirometry. Use the case to connect airway mechanism, expected obstructive measurements and the limitation of the available evidence.

stations.title: Locate the SA node

parts.answer: Near the junction of SVC and right atrium at the superior end of the crista/sulcus terminalis.

parts.answer: Initiates the normal cardiac pacemaker rhythm.

stations.title: Respiratory epithelial cells

stations.title: Olfactory supporting cells

parts.answer: Supporting nuclei are more apical; basal-cell nuclei lie near the basal lamina.

stations.title: Posterior tracheal wall

stations.title: Mitral regurgitation trace

parts.prompt: Identify the valve lesion suggested by the large atrial systolic v-wave in this tracing.

parts.answer: Blood regurgitates from the contracting left ventricle into the left atrium.

stations.remember: A giant v-wave is a systolic atrial pressure rise, not atrial contraction. Regurgitation means the normal sealed isovolumetric assumption is impaired.

stations.title: Aortic stenosis pressure gradient

parts.prompt: What lesion produces a large systolic LV-to-aortic pressure gradient as shown?

parts.answer: The ventricle must generate extra pressure to eject through the narrowed aortic valve.

stations.remember: Compare simultaneous LV and aortic systolic pressures; a large gradient across the outflow valve is the central clue.

stations.title: Mitral stenosis pressure separation

parts.prompt: Which valve lesion causes persistently elevated LA pressure relative to LV during filling?

stations.remember: The mitral valve normally opens during ventricular filling. Obstruction raises upstream LA and pulmonary venous pressure.

stations.title: Aortic regurgitation trace

parts.prompt: Which lesion gives the low aortic diastolic pressure and wide pulse pressure shown?
In which phase does the abnormal aorta-to-LV flow occur?

stations.remember: The worksheet reverses systole/diastole in two question stems. Low aortic pressure reflects diastolic runoff; systolic pressure can rise with the enlarged stroke volume.

stations.title: Wide pulse pressure

parts.prompt: Using the stated source-case BP160/40 mmHg, calculate pulse pressure.
What happens to LV volume loading in significant aortic regurgitation?
parts.answer: It increases: the LV receives normal venous return plus regurgitant aortic volume.

stations.remember: Use the supplied case values rather than guessing from a low-resolution axis. Volume overload can raise LV end-diastolic volume.

stations.title: Club-cell function

parts.prompt: Identify the non-ciliated dome-shaped secretory cells indicated in this bronchiolar field.

parts.answer: CC16; airway epithelial protection/immunomodulation, with a progenitor role in repair.

stations.title: Lamellar bodies

parts.prompt: Name the organelles with concentric lamellar material in the electron micrograph.
Which alveolar cell stores and secretes their product?
parts.answer: Type II pneumocyte; the product is pulmonary surfactant.

stations.remember: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension; DPPC is its principal surface-tension-reducing phospholipid.

stations.title: Alveolar and septal macrophages

parts.prompt: Identify the irregular pigment-laden phagocytic cells.
What does hemosiderin in alveolar macrophages indicate?
parts.answer: Prior phagocytosis of extravasated red blood cells, as can occur with pulmonary congestion/left-sided heart failure.

stations.remember: Alveolar macrophages act in airspaces; septal macrophages lie in connective tissue. Pigment alone must be interpreted in context.

stations.title: Air-blood barrier

parts.prompt: Name the two cell types bounding the thin air-blood barrier.
parts.answer: Type I pneumocyte and capillary endothelial cell.

parts.prompt: What happens to their basal laminae in its thin portion?
parts.answer: They are closely apposed and often fused.

stations.remember: Gas crosses the alveolar surface lining, thin type I cell, basal laminae and capillary endothelium; thick septal connective tissue increases diffusion distance.

stations.title: Alveolar connections

parts.prompt: What are the small channels through interalveolar septa connecting neighbouring alveoli?

parts.answer: They can permit collateral air movement from neighbouring alveoli.

stations.remember: Do not confuse alveolar pores with a bronchiole or an alveolar duct.

stations.title: Enlarged alveolar spaces

parts.prompt: Identify the main structural abnormality.
parts.answer: Enlarged airspaces with destruction of alveolar septa, consistent with emphysema.

parts.prompt: How does this affect gas-exchange surface area and elastic recoil?

stations.remember: Emphysema is destructive enlargement, not simply temporary alveolar expansion during inspiration.

corrections.issue: Eustachian valve is at the IVC, not SVC.
Membranous septum is small; the one-third fraction is not used. Coronary ostia are in aortic sinus walls, not valve cusps.
Circumflex is a principal branch of LCA.
LAD supplies anterior two-thirds; PDA posterior one-third, not the reversed fractions.
Glottis is vocal folds plus rima glottidis; arytenoids are not added to its definition.
Innermost intercostals are not assigned the duplicated subcostales attachments.
Q6 repeats Q5 answers despite asking cells and function; replaced with independently stated learning points.
Left lower-lobe segment number list is inconsistent; it is not graded.
Mock Q11 label D is explicitly uncertain and is not graded.
Two aortic-regurgitation question stems reverse systole/diastole. Practice uses diastolic aortic runoff and widened pulse pressure.

summary: The supplied committee walkthrough describes around 20 stations with 90 seconds per station and two rest stations. Confirm the final arrangements from the exam announcement.
Most questions have two parts: identify the structure, then give its function, supply, relation or distinguishing features.
At the bell, move immediately. During rest stations you may revisit written answers, without seeing other stations.
Bring a pen/pencil and lab coat. The walkthrough prohibits devices in the holding area and touching/moving models. Follow the current proctor instructions.
walkthrough.note: Committee guidance, not an official guarantee of station count, content, venue or assessment weight.
